food.text: The ancient Maya diet centered on four domesticated crops: maize, squash, beans and chili peppers. The first three are often called the "Three Sisters" because, eaten together, they complement one another in providing necessary nutrients. Maize was the central part of the diet and figured prominently in Maya mythology.

Once nixtamalized, Maya maize was typically ground on a metate and prepared in many ways. Tortillas, cooked on a comal and used to wrap foods such as meat and beans, were common. Tamales were made of corn dough, often with a filling, wrapped in a corn husk and steam-cooked.

During the Classic period, the Maya moved goods along long-distance trade routes, such as one running from the Motagua River to the Caribbean Sea and then north up the coast to Yucatán. Basic trade goods may have included obsidian, salt and cacao, while jade, fine ceramics and quetzal feathers marked elite status.

Much of the ancient Maya food supply grew in agricultural fields and forest gardens known as pet kot. The name comes from the stones that characteristically surrounded the gardens: pet means "circular" and kot means "wall of loose stones".

Beans and corn are deficient in different essential amino acids, but they complement each other. When eaten in combination, they provide a complete protein source. Common beans, Phaseolus vulgaris, have long been a component of the Mexican diet alongside corn.

Mesoamerican chocolate was made by grinding toasted cacao beans, sometimes with parched corn, and mixing the powder with water. The drink was beaten with a wooden whisk until foamy. Vanilla orchid pods or honey were used as flavor enhancers.
Archaeological evidence suggests that Chapalote-Nal-Tel was the dominant species of maize among the ancient Maya. It is likely that other varieties were being exploited as well.

art.text: During Period III of Teotihuacan, which lasted from 350 to 650 CE, artisans made funeral masks mainly from green stone. They covered the masks with mosaics of turquoise, shell or obsidian. The masks were highly uniform in nature.

Teotihuacan is known for the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon, among the most architecturally significant pyramids in the pre-Columbian Americas. In Period III, from 350 to 650 CE, the city held around 100,000 inhabitants and 2,000 buildings within 18 square kilometers.

Maya ceramics are the most commonly surviving type of Maya art. The Maya did not know the potter's wheel, so they built vessels by coiling rolled strips of clay. The pottery was unglazed but often burnished, and it was painted with clay slips blended with minerals and coloured clays.

Archaeologists found a jar in Guatemala, attributed to the Maya of the Late Classic Era (600-900 AD), that depicts a musical instrument. When a reproduction is played, it makes a sound virtually identical to a jaguar's growl. It is the only stringed instrument known in the Americas before European instruments arrived.

Period III at Teotihuacan, from 350 to 650 CE, saw a massive reconstruction of buildings. The Temple of the Feathered Serpent, which dated to the previous period, was covered with a plaza with rich sculptural decoration.

Extremely fine ceramic figurines have been excavated from Late Classic tombs on Jaina Island, in northern Yucatán. They stand from 10 to 25 centimetres high and were hand modelled with exquisite detail.

Between the late 6th and late 7th century, Tikal saw a lapse in inscriptions and large-scale construction, known as the Tikal hiatus. No new stelae were erected, and public sculpture was widely and deliberately mutilated. The hiatus followed Tikal's comprehensive defeat by Calakmul and Caracol in AD 562, a defeat that seems to have resulted in the capture and sacrifice of the king of Tikal. Tikal was not sacked, but its power was broken, and some of its population may have been forcibly relocated to Caracol.

The Ik-style polychrome ceramic corpus, which includes finely painted plates and cylindrical vessels, originated in Late Classic Motul de San José. It features hieroglyphs painted in a pink or pale red colour and scenes with dancers wearing masks.

In the 8th century, the rulers of Tikal collected monuments from across the city. They erected them in front of the North Acropolis, decades after the hiatus had already ended in 682 with a new dated monument.

Painted cylinder vases of the Late Classic period are the most common place to see decapitated human heads worn or presented as trophy heads, and they usually involve the Hero Twins or some type of Creation myth. Maya images of trophy heads show them held by the hair, which was a sign of disrespect, or hanging upside down. Blood or possibly other fluids are shown flowing from the neck, eyes or mouth. Heads were usually worn upright with the eyes open on a belt at the small of the back.

The south-central panel of the Classic era South Ballcourt at El Tajín shows the rain god piercing his penis. The blood flows into and replenishes a vat of pulque, an alcoholic ritual drink, linking the drink to sacrifice and renewal.

Ik-style vessels are distinctive for realistically showing subjects as they appeared in life. Their scenes show courtly life from the Petén region in the 8th century AD, including diplomatic meetings, feasting, bloodletting, warriors and the sacrifice of prisoners of war.

By the late 8th and early 9th century, activity at Tikal slowed. Impressive architecture was still built, but few hieroglyphic inscriptions refer to later rulers. Tikal was abandoned by the end of the 10th century.

war.text: The Classic period of Mesoamerica ran from 250 to 900 CE and was dominated by the influence of Teotihuacan. Competition between the different Mesoamerican states led to continuous warfare. In the Maya region, city-states were involved in bloody wars with changing alliances, and the Tikal–Calakmul wars stretched over more than half a millennium. Toward the end of the late Classic, many Maya cities were burned and abandoned to the jungle.

The macuahuitl was a Mesoamerican close-combat weapon: a wooden sword with several obsidian blades embedded in its sides. Its use as a weapon is attested from the first millennium CE. Later it was used by the Aztec, Maya, Mixtec, Toltec and other peoples.
Teotihuacan grew to perhaps as many as 200,000 inhabitants at its height. It lasted until around AD 700, when it was burned and vandalised.

Around 500 to 600 CE, speakers of Proto-Nahuan moved south into central Mexico. Their arrival coincided with the decline of Teotihuacan and a period of turmoil and mass migration. Scientists have speculated that they might have been involved in the empire's fall.

Teotihuacan dominated the Valley of Mexico until the early 8th century. Little is known of its political structure, because the Teotihuacanos left no written records. Around 600 CE other city-states may have economically strangled it, trapped in the centre of the valley without access to trade routes. People kept living there for another century and a half, but the city was eventually destroyed and abandoned, and it was burned, its inhabitants taking refuge in places such as Culhuacán and Azcapotzalco.

The Postclassic was once presented as a period of warlike states set against the pacifist states of the Classic. New interpretations of archaeological evidence from Teotihuacan and the Maya show that war was also important in the Classic period.

The Toltec hegemony of Tula dominated central Mexico through the early Postclassic, from the 10th to the 13th century. In the preceding period the Classic order was ending: Monte Albán in Oaxaca disappeared around 850, and like La Quemada and Teotihuacan it was burned and abandoned, for reasons that are still unclear. The fall of Tula later checked the power of the zuyuano system, which finally broke down with the dissolution of the League of Mayapán and the Mixtec state and the abandonment of Tula.

The badly eroded Altar 21 at Caracol described how Tikal suffered a disastrous defeat in a major war in April 562. Tikal's king seems to have been captured and sacrificed, and widespread deliberate mutilation of public sculpture followed. After its great victory, Caracol grew rapidly, and some of Tikal's population may have been forcibly relocated there.

Teotihuacan exported fine obsidian tools found throughout Mesoamerica. Around 550 CE its major monuments were sacked and systematically burned, and the sculptures inside palatial structures such as Xalla were shattered. Its collapse might be related to the extreme weather events of 535–536, which may have caused lengthy droughts and famine: skeletons from the 6th century show a rise in juveniles with evidence of malnutrition.

Obsidian can produce an edge sharper than high quality steel razor blades, and the macuahuitl was capable of inflicting serious lacerations from the rows of obsidian blades set in its sides. According to the article, it was sharp enough to decapitate a man. Several obsidian mines lay near the Valley of Mexico, including the Sierra de las Navajas, or Razor Mountains, named for their obsidian deposits.

It is believed that Maya soldiers did not patrol in large armies but in many smaller groups or raiding parties. Most battles were driven by the desire for domination and the intention to intimidate other cities.

Victors often took captives back to their cities and used them for ritual sacrifice. Some captives were bound or hindered so they could not fairly compete in a winner-take-all ballcourt match. The loser was beheaded, and the victor might keep his head as a trophy to confirm victory and establish his city's dominance.
The name macuahuitl comes from the Nahuatl language and means "hand-wood". The weapon predates the Aztecs, and tools made from obsidian fragments were used by some of the earliest Mesoamericans.

literature.text: Most texts written in the indigenous scripts of Mesoamerica, such as Maya, date to about 600 to 900 CE. That places much of the region's surviving writing within this era. The oldest Mesoamerican texts, Olmec and Zapotec, are far older, at about 1000 BCE.
Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica made folding-book manuscripts from amate. Few codices survive from before the Spanish conquest of Mexico and Yucatán, because of Spanish Christian book burnings.

In Mesoamerica, writing, drawing and making pictures were seen as closely related, if not identical, concepts. Classic Maya used a single word, tz'iib', for both writing and drawing. Nahuatl likewise used tlàcuiloa for both.

Modern scholars struggle to tell whether a Mesoamerican inscription represents spoken language or is meant as a descriptive drawing. Pictures are sometimes read phonetically, and texts meant to be read are sometimes very pictorial. Many scripts use the rebus principle and a highly conventionalised set of symbols.

The Zapotecs of Monte Alban, who began around 500 BC in the Oaxaca Valley, had a writing system and a calendar, as the Olmecs did. Monte Alban grew to around 25,000 residents around AD 200. By AD 900 it was deserted for unknown reasons.

Nahuatl has been spoken in central Mexico since at least the seventh century AD. It was written down only after the Spanish conquest, when missionaries introduced the Latin script and Nahuatl became a literary language. Chronicles, poetry and codices followed in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Toltec people of Tula, active in central Mexico around the 10th century, are thought to have been Nahuatl speakers. Nahuatl later became a language of literature, with its Tenochtitlan variety known as Classical Nahuatl.

Scholars still do not know what language the people and rulers of Teotihuacan spoke. Possible candidates are Nahuatl, Totonac and Mixe–Zoque. Terrence Kaufman argues that Nahuatl is unlikely, because Proto-Nahuan did not enter Mesoamerica until around the time of the fall of Teotihuacan, about 600 AD.

science.text: The Maya combined a 260-day count, the Tzolkin, with a 365-day vague solar year called the Haabʼ. Together they formed a synchronized cycle lasting 52 Haabʼ, known as the Calendar Round.
Metallurgy emerged relatively late in Mesoamerica. Distinctive metal works appear in West Mexico by roughly 800 CE, and perhaps as early as 600 CE.

Metalworking techniques likely reached Mesoamerica by moving northward from Central or South America along maritime trade routes. The people who received them worked a wide range of materials, including alloys of copper-silver, copper-arsenic, copper-tin and copper-arsenic-tin.
In the 10th century, metallurgy arrived in Mesoamerica from South America. The Maya then began to make small objects in gold, silver and copper.

The earliest and most diverse metal finds in Mesoamerica come from West Mexico, in a belt along the Pacific coast from Guerrero to Nayarit. This suggests the region was a nucleus of metallurgy, from which technique, form and style could have spread across Mesoamerica.

Mesoamerican metal items fall into three classes: utilitarian objects, personal ornaments, and ceremonial or ritual objects. The last two make up most of the distinctly Mesoamerican artifacts, because metals played an important role in the sacred and symbolic realms.
The Maya generally hammered sheet metal into objects such as beads, bells and discs. These were small pieces, made once metalworking had reached the Maya region.

Scholars such as Dorothy Hosler suggest ancient Mesoamericans were unique in their attention to the aesthetic properties of metals, such as the brilliant sounds and colors of moving metal objects. Because metallurgy emerged late, it was a novelty and likely became a marker of elite status.

Different Maya regions tracked the new year with different Year Bearers. During the Late Classic period, Campeche used the Tzolkʼin days that coincided with 1 Pop: Akʼbʼal, Lamat, Bʼen and Edznab. The classic system, found at Tikal, was different.

Mesoamerican smiths may have made alloys mainly for their color: tin gives vivid gold tones, and high arsenic gives silver shades. Some West Mexican artifacts contain tin or arsenic at up to 23 weight percent, though 2 to 5 percent is typically enough for strength.

In 2024, researchers analysed the genomes of ancient individuals from the Maya city of Chichén Itzá, dating to around AD 500–900. They grouped with modern Amerindian populations, especially the present-day Maya, when compared with blood samples from 68 people in Tixcacaltuyub, Mexico.

politics.text: The Classic Period was dominated by numerous independent city-states in the Maya region. It also saw the beginnings of political unity in central Mexico and the Yucatán. Competition between the Mesoamerican states led to continuous warfare, and the Maya cities were drawn into bloody wars with changing alliances. In 732 Tikal finished defeating its rivals, ending with Calakmul itself, an event marked by the sacrifice of Yuknom Cheen's son in Tikal.

The city-state of Monte Albán dominated the Valley of Oaxaca until the late Classic. It left limited records in the Zapotec script, which is still mostly undeciphered. Around 850 it disappeared, ending the Classic period in Oaxaca; it was burned and abandoned, for reasons that are still unclear.

According to the Anales de Cuauhtitlan, Tollan-Xicocotitlan was ruled from 923 to 947 by the priest-king Cē Ācatl Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, who was born in 895 at Michatlauhco. He preached against human sacrifice, arguing that the supreme deity whose name he took was not pleased by ritual killings. According to Sahagún, he was tricked into drinking pulque and got drunk with his sister, the priestess Quetzalpetlatl; humiliated, he left Tollan in 947, and on the Gulf coast took a canoe and immolated himself.

The Classic Maya civilization began to collapse in the mid-eighth century. By around 925, about when the Toltecs began to migrate into the Maya area, most major Maya cities in the Yucatán Peninsula had already been abandoned because of food shortages and peasant revolts.

The end of the Classic period came at different times across Mesoamerica. In the Gulf it came with the decline of El Tajín in 800, and in the Maya area with the abandonment of the highland cities in the 9th century. Toward the end of the late Classic many Maya cities were burned and abandoned to the jungle, and Monte Albán and Teotihuacan met the same fate. In central Mexico the period ended with the fall of the regional centers of the late Classic, toward 900.

Some authors, such as historian Vicente Riva Palacio, argue that Quetzalcoatl died in 931. They say his death triggered political instability in Tollan and a Toltec migration around 981, especially to the Yucatan Peninsula, where many settled at Uxmal.

Traditional accounts say that at the end of the tenth century a religious war broke out in Tollan between the cult of Tezcatlipoca and the supporters of Quetzalcoatl. Followers of Quetzalcoatl, mostly of Nonoalca background, did not favour large-scale human sacrifice, which Ce Acatl Topiltzin had largely suppressed during his reign. Followers of Tezcatlipoca, mostly of Chichimeca background, regarded the sacrifices as an essential part of their religion.

According to archaeologist Román Piña Chan, the Itza introduced the cult of Quetzalcoatl, known as Kukulkan in Yucatan, around 987 AD. The Itza were of mixed Putún Maya and Toltec descent. They had welcomed immigrants from Tollan and adopted the religious teachings of the Toltecs.

philosophy.text: After Teotihuacan fell around 600 AD, the cult of the feathered serpent spread to new religious and political centers in central Mexico. Xochicalco, Cacaxtla and Cholula all show prominent feathered-serpent iconography.

Maya cosmology held that the universe had three tiers: sky, earth and underworld. Each layer was divided into its own levels, with transitional zones between them. Caves could serve as a transitional site, bringing humans and deities from the earth to the underworld.

Teotihuacan's Great Goddess is thought to have been a goddess of the underworld, darkness, the earth, water, war, and possibly even creation itself. She appears peculiar to Teotihuacan, and does not appear outside the city except where Teotihuacanos settled.

Worship of a Feathered Serpent is first documented at Teotihuacan, and by the Late Classic period (600–900 AD) veneration appears to have spread throughout Mesoamerica. In the Maya area the deity was roughly equivalent to Kukulkan and Gukumatz, names that also translate as feathered serpent.

Mesoamerican peoples considered the jaguar, the owl and especially the spider to be creatures of darkness, often found in caves and at night. Because the Great Goddess is frequently depicted with all of them, scholars see this as support for her underworld connections.

Maya mythological tradition credits the deity Itzamna with bringing knowledge of the calendrical system to the ancestral Maya, along with writing in general and other foundational aspects of Maya culture. This tradition is reconstructed from Late Classic and Postclassic inscriptions.

Xochicalco was an important fortressed commercial and religious center, and nearly all its standing architecture dates to the Epiclassic period (AD 700–900). Feathered-serpent iconography is prominent there, and its Temple of the Feathered Serpent was restored in 1910 by Leopoldo Batres.
The Great Goddess left very little trace in the Valley of Mexico's later Toltec culture. Still, an earth goddess image has been identified on Stela 1 from Xochicalco, a Toltec contemporary.

In the Popol Vuh, Hun Hunahpu is killed by the Lords of Xibalba, and his severed head is placed in a calabash tree. To the Maya of the Classic period, Hun Hunahpu may have represented the maize god. Although the Popol Vuh states unequivocally that his severed head became a calabash, some scholars believe the calabash to be interchangeable with a cacao pod or an ear of corn. In this line, his decapitation and sacrifice correspond to harvesting corn, and to the sacrifices accompanying planting and harvesting, which also tie to Maya astronomy and the calendar, since the cycles of the moon and sun determined the crop seasons.

In ancient Maya cities, offerings and sacrificial implements were stored and buried in caches below floors, stelae and altars. The intention may often have been a dedication to a specific religious purpose, rather than an offering to a divine recipient.

culture.text: The Classic period (250-900 CE) is usually seen as the stage when Mesoamerican arts, science, urbanism, architecture and social organization reached their peak. Highly sophisticated arts such as stuccowork, sculptural reliefs, mural painting, pottery and lapidary developed and spread during this era.

Many elements of Maya culture were shared across Mesoamerica, including two calendars, a base 20 number system, the cultivation of corn and the myth of the fifth sun. Human sacrifice was shared too, as was the worship of the Feathered Serpent and of the rain god, who in the Yucatec Maya language is called Chaac. Confirmation that the Maya practiced human sacrifice and ritual cannibalism came much later, for example from the murals of Bonampak.

Monte Albán dominated the Valley of Oaxaca until the late Classic period. It left limited records in the Zapotec script, which is still mostly undeciphered. It reached its apex around 750 and then, for reasons still unclear, succumbed toward the end of the 9th century: it was burned and abandoned. In Oaxaca, the Classic period is considered to end with its disappearance around 850.

The Pipil were the last indigenous civilization to arrive in El Salvador, coming from 900 CE onwards. They speak Nahuat, or Pipil, which is still spoken today though endangered. They are considered descendants of the Toltecs and relatives of the Aztecs.

Around the 10th century AD, metallurgy arrived in Mesoamerica from South America. The Maya began making small objects in gold, silver and copper. They generally hammered sheet metal into beads, bells and discs.

Although the Pipil are related to the Aztecs, their mythology is more closely related to that of their Maya neighbors. Oral tradition says the Pipil were adopted by the Ch'orti' and Poqomam Maya people during the Pipil exodus in the 9th century CE.

Teotihuacan's apogee and population growth encouraged migration north and commerce with distant Oasisamerica. Northern Mesoamerica was part of the cultural area only during the Classic era (150-750 CE). Its people were so dependent on good weather for farming, which was only possible by channelling surface water and storing rain, that a prolonged drought and invasions of Aridoamerican people made them abandon the region in the middle of the 8th century. Agriculture and the social system collapsed, and the survivors migrated towards the West, the Gulf, and the Center of Mexico.

Beginning around 650 AD, most settlements in the Tula region were abandoned as Teotihuacan declined. The Coyotlatelco rose as the dominant culture, and it was with them that Tula, as it relates to the Toltec, was founded along with a number of hilltop communities.

At Tula Grande, sunken colonnaded halls served as places to engage with regional and long-distance trade networks, and possibly for diplomacy. Imported goods there show the Toltecs traded with sites throughout Mesoamerica, and Tula shares ceramic and ritual figurine styles with regions such as Socunusco.
